name: SynapTech AerSense Air Quality Monitor Implant
body_location: nasal submucosal — bilateral nasal passage lining, with secondary node at ethmoid sinus
description:
The AerSense is a submucosal nasal implant consisting of a bilateral array of micro-sensors embedded in the nasal passage lining, connected to a processing node seated in the ethmoid sinus cavity. The sensor array continuously samples inhaled air for a broad spectrum of compounds: particulate matter by size class (PM1, PM2.5, PM10), volatile organic compounds, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone, common industrial solvents, biological aerosols including mold spores and airborne pathogens, and a user-configurable panel of personal allergens. Data is processed locally and delivered as a real-time ambient air quality index to a linked BCI or companion display. When the system detects concentrations above user-defined thresholds, it delivers a discreet haptic alert via a small node behind the ear — a gentle pulse that escalates in frequency with severity. The AerSense does not filter air in any meaningful mechanical sense; it is a sensor platform, not a respirator. However, the nasal sensor array does carry a mild antimicrobial coating that reduces pathogen adhesion to the implant surfaces themselves.

Meridian 88's air quality is, to put it charitably, variable. The lower Shelf districts sit beneath industrial transit corridors, near aging manufacturing infrastructure, and adjacent to the lake reclamation zones where remediation chemistry produces its own complex outgassing. Tier 1 and Tier 2 residents have historically had no real-time awareness of what they were breathing — the city's public air quality monitoring network is sparse and notoriously slow to update. The AerSense changed this for hundreds of thousands of residents. Knowing that the air in a particular corridor is spiking with diesel particulate, or that a building's ventilation is pushing elevated CO, or that the market district has a mold bloom after the spring floods — this is actionable information that saves lives and reduces chronic illness. Parents install it in children. Couriers use it to route around industrial air events. Workers in chemical-adjacent industries are often required by their employers to carry one as a safety compliance measure.
installation_requirements: Outpatient ENT-adjacent clinic or licensed installer; 25-minute procedure under local anesthetic; nasal placement is non-surgical but requires trained installer; mild post-procedure congestion for 2–3 days
maintenance: Sensor array recalibration annually; allergen panel updates via app sync; antimicrobial coating refresh recommended every 18 months at a SynapTech kiosk; ethmoid node battery replacement every 4 years

side_effects: First week includes mild nasal congestion and occasional sneezing as mucosa adapts to sensor array
Some users report heightened odor sensitivity — the sensors do not enhance smell directly, but increased awareness of air composition creates a perceptual effect
Rare: minor sinus pressure when the ethmoid node is processing high compound-density air samples
Occasional phantom alerts in very clean air environments during initial calibration, typically resolves within two weeks
cultural_context: The AerSense has become deeply associated with Shelf-district survival culture in a way that gives it a different valence across tiers. In Tier 1 communities, wearing one is an act of self-preservation and is regarded with the same quiet seriousness as carrying a water filter. There are informal neighborhood networks where AerSense users share real-time air data through mesh apps, creating a grassroots air quality monitoring system that rivals anything the city officially provides — and is often more accurate. In Tier 3 and above, it shades into wellness culture and urban anxiety management. Tier 4 and 5 residents in clean-air Spire environments occasionally install it as a status-adjacent health gesture, which Tier 1 residents find somewhere between amusing and offensive. The phrase 'canary in a clean room' is Shelf slang for a Spire person who installed an AerSense and has never actually needed it.
known_users: Shelf district residents in industrial air corridors
people with respiratory conditions or severe allergies
story_hooks: Dozens of AerSense users in a Shelf neighborhood received simultaneous alerts for a compound that shouldn't exist outside a sealed laboratory — someone has released something into the ventilation system of a residential block, and the only early warning came from residents' personal implants, not city monitoring

A corporate lawyer is building a class action case against a manufacturing corponation using aggregated AerSense logs from thousands of Shelf residents as evidence of chronic illegal emissions — the corponation is now quietly attempting to push a firmware update that would recalibrate the relevant sensors out of accurate range
